JSON: Name: mcf_hartmann_hyperspectral_wfs Title: Single-shot hyperspectral wavefront sensing using a multicore-fiber Hartmann mask to recover spatio-spectral wavefront cubes from broadband illumination Short Hypothesis: Placing a multicore fiber (MCF) as a Hartmann-style mask at a short imaging distance encodes wavelength-dependent speckle diversity and local wavefront-gradient displacements such that a single broadband camera acquisition followed by SVD-regularized inversion and multi-scale registration recovers per-wavelength wavefronts with RMS error ≤ λ/50 relative to sequential monochromatic wavefront measurements across a 100 nm bandwidth. Related Work: Existing wavefront sensing approaches include: (a) conventional Hartmann/Shack–Hartmann sensors and lateral-shearing interferometers which measure monochromatic wavefronts or assume achromatic wavefronts, therefore providing only spectrally averaged results under broadband illumination; (b) multispectral methods that split discrete spectral lines onto conventional WFS using Fabry–Perot etalons or gratings, enabling single-shot multispectral measurement for a few discrete wavelengths but not contiguous spectra; (c) hyperspectral imaging chains that combine coded-aperture compressive cameras (CASSI) with phase retrieval to reconstruct spectral fields, which require complex cascaded optics, iterative phaseretrieval and low spatial sampling; (d) thin diffusers or scattering media used as compact wavefront masks that exploit the angular memory effect, but when thick or multiply-scattering they display increased spectral correlation width or reduced angular memory, limiting wavefront sensitivity or spectral discrimination. Limitations common to these approaches are: requirement for cascaded or bulky dispersive optics for contiguous spectra, trade-offs between spectral and spatial sampling that reduce either resolution or throughput, reduced angular memory in thick/ multimode scattering media, and high experimental complexity or poor single-shot capability for continuous hyperspectral wavefront reconstruction. Abstract: We present a single-shot hyperspectral wavefront sensing pipeline that combines Hartmann-deflectometry principles with a multicore-fiber (MCF) used as a compact Hartmann mask. The MCF provides a short-distance angular memory effect that converts local wavefront gradients into speckle displacements and a limited spectral correlation width that encodes spectral content into statistically independent speckle realizations. A calibration of monochromatic reference speckles and a reconstruction pipeline based on truncated-SVD inversion and multi-scale optical-flow registration recover per-wavelength intensity and phase across contiguous spectra from a single broadband camera exposure. The main contribution is a compact, single-element optical encoding that achieves tunable trade-offs between spatial and spectral resolution while preserving single-shot acquisition. Expected outcomes include quantitative per-wavelength wavefront maps (metrology-grade accuracy), single-pulse characterization of high-power laser beams, and high-resolution multispectral phase microscopy without cascaded dispersive optics. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Controlled optics dataset: three wedge prisms (NBK7) with nominal deviation angles 2°, 4°, 6° and two afocal lens-pair systems (f=50 mm in NBK7 and SF11) imaged across 500–800 nm continuous range. Acquire sequential monochromatic ground-truth scans at 1 nm steps using a narrow-line source (5 nm linewidth) and monochromator; acquire single-shot broadband multiplexed images using a broadband source (bandwidths 40 nm and 100 nm). (2) High-power single-pulse dataset: single-shot acquisitions of Apollon laser pulses (650–1000 nm central) at the LFA beamline using the MCF-WFS in-line; collect sequential narrowband scans where feasible for ground truth. (3) Microscopy phantom dataset: 5.2 μm PMMA beads in aqueous sucrose solution with added chromophore; multispectral illumination channels 480/20 nm, 580/10 nm, 690/10 nm; acquire sequential narrowband scans and single-shot multiplexed images. Baselines: (A) Sequential monochromatic Hartmann/Shack–Hartmann wavefront sensing (scanned narrowband) as reference ground truth; (B) Broadband Shack–Hartmann assuming achromatic wavefront; (C) Coded-aperture hyperspectral + phase-retrieval pipeline (CASSI-like) with comparable pixel budget; (D) Thin-diffuser WFS single-shot approach. Evaluation metrics: per-wavelength RMS OPD error (nm) relative to sequential ground truth; peak-to-valley (PtV) OPD; tip/tilt RMSE (μrad); spectral RMSE of reconstructed power spectrum; spectral resolution (minimum resolvable Δλ); spectral correlation width δλ measured from calibration; spatial resolution (μm) from bead PSF and modulation transfer; reconstruction SNR and PSNR for intensity; robustness: RMSE vs. input SNR (dB); computational metrics: inversion time and memory. Experimental setup: MCF variants lengths L = {1 cm, 10 cm, 50 cm} (to vary δλ), imaging distances d = {6 mm, 88 mm, 90 mm} (microscopy vs metrology modes), microscope objectives ×10 (NA 0.3) and ×20 (NA 0.4), camera pixel sampling set so single-fiber diffraction spot spans ≈12×12 pixels; calibration: capture reference speckles R(λ) at 1 nm steps across spectral band; form measurement matrix Re and solve M = Re X + noise using truncated-SVD inversion with half-Gaussian singular-value filtering and iterative multi-scale optical-flow registration for displacement maps; set Nλ (number of spectral channels) from 5 to 40 to probe spatio-spectral trade-off. Trials and statistics: repeat each measurement configuration N=20 independent acquisitions to quantify mean and standard deviation. Ablation studies: (i) vary MCF length to quantify δλ influence on spectral resolution and OPD error; (ii) sweep d to quantify sensitivity vs spatial resolution trade-off; (iii) compare inversion variants: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse vs truncated-SVD vs sparsity-constrained inversion; (iv) enable/disable multi-scale registration to measure effect on large-displacement accuracy; (v) vary Nλ to determine condition number threshold κ and reconstruction stability. Risk Factors and Limitations: Limited angular memory: few-mode cores or inter-core coupling in MCF reduce angular memory range and thus restrict maximum reconstructible local wavefront slope and dynamic range. Spectral-correlation dependence on fiber manufacturing: δλ depends on uncontrolled longitudinal pathlength dispersion between cores and may vary between MCF samples, limiting reproducibility and tunability. Calibration sensitivity and stability: accurate per-wavelength reference speckles are required; relay optics chromatic aberrations and mechanical drift will bias reconstructions; frequent recalibration may be required. Matrix inversion ill-conditioning: when requested number of spectral channels Nλ approaches available independent spatial modes M, the calibration matrix becomes ill-conditioned, producing amplification of noise and requiring SVD truncation that reduces effective spectral resolution. Spatial resolution limits: inter-core spacing and free-space propagation set lower bound on resolvable spatial frequency; high spatial resolution requires short d and denser core bundle not always available. Missing-data regions: central intensity nulls or saturated pixels lead to unreliable local OPD and require interpolation, reducing local accuracy. Computational cost and latency: SVD-based inversion and multi-scale registration are computationally expensive for large fields or high Nλ, limiting real-time operation without substantial compute resources. Applicability constraints: method assumes deterministic, reproducible speckle statistics and fails for strongly scattering/thick media where angular memory breaks down, and for samples with rapid temporal fluctuations during single-shot exposure beyond detector integration.
